What is UNIX?
A trademark for any of several computer operating systems developed at AT&T Bell Labs.

A computer operating system or interface that bears a significant resemblance to UNIX.

Associated with UNIX.  “The UNIX Shell.”

UNIX History, Part 1
1969	Version 1.  Written by Dennis Ritchie and Ken Thompson for the DEC PDP-7.

1973	Version 4.  This was the first version written in C.  The translation into C made UNIX portable, and was fundamental to its eventual success.

1975	Version 6.  This was the first version widely available outside AT&T, and the first version that was ported to several architectures.

1979	Version 7.  The common ancestor of most commercial UNIX versions, version 7 was ported widely and documented in the famous blue and green books.  These were the first generally available references to UNIX.

UNIX History, Part 2
Early 1980s
           University of California at Berkeley was contracted by DARPA to add virtual memory support to UNIX for use on DEC VAX computers.   Berkeley was later contracted to add Internet style networking to UNIX.  “Berkeley UNIX”, aka BSD, became very popular with academia and began to diverge from AT&T UNIX.

1983	System V.  AT&T released this version with much fanfare, declaring it to be the UNIX standard.  Many commercial versions were based on it.  The Great BSD vs AT&T War had begun.

UNIX History, Part 3
1985	BSD versions 4.2 and 4.3 were used as the basis for many commercial UNIX releases, including SunOS and Ultrix.  Many AT&T based releases include  “Berkeley enhancements”.

1988	Sun, AT&T and Microsoft merged their versions of UNIX into System V, Release 4 (SVR4).  The BSD vs AT&T War ended with no winner, because...

1988	Several companies, unhappy with SVR4, form the Open Software Foundation.  OSF creates OSF/1, a UNIX clone based on Mach from Carnegie Mellon University.  The Great SVR4 vs OSF/1 War had begun...

UNIX History, Part 4
1992    Unix System Laboratories bought by Novell, ending 23 years of control by AT&T over UNIX.  Novell pledges to make UNIX a major desktop platform, fully integrated with Netware.  Move is widely viewed as a response to Microsoft’s upcoming Windows NT.

1993    UNIX International and the OSF kiss and make up, with various members of each forming COSE, the Common Open Software Environment.   Move is widely viewed as a response to Microsoft’s upcoming Windows NT.

What makes it UNIX?
Multitasking

Multiuser

Networked

Portable

Multitasking
Multitasking is the ability of a computer system to execute more than one program at a time.   UNIX has always been a multitasking system.

Modern PC operating systems like Microsoft Windows 3.0 and Mac System 7 feature co-operative multitasking.  Under co-operative multitasking, an application must voluntarily give up the system to another task.

UNIX, and PC operating systems such as OS/2 2.0 and Windows NT, use pre-emptive multitasking, under which the system can grab control from one application and give it to another.

Multiuser
A multiuser system is one that can be used by more than one person at a time.  Multiuser systems are inherently multitasking.

A multiuser system requires some method of determining the identity of any given user.  This login name is used to determine ownership of files and to control access to data and programs.

LAN operating systems such as Novell and LAN Manager incorporate many of the ideas of multiuser systems.  Microsoft’s upcoming Windows NT is  multi-user, with restrictions.

NetworkedTCP/IP
Networking in UNIX is based almost entirely on the Berkeley TCP/IP implementation.

The cheap availability of the Berkeley networking code led to its incorporation into many commercial versions of UNIX and to the standardization of the sockets interface.

Every important networking standard is supported under UNIX:  Ethernet/802.3, TCP/IP, DECnet, Novell, Token Ring, XNS, etc.

Networkeduucp
The uucp program copies files from one UNIX computer to another over a serial port.  This basic transport layer provided the basis of the earliest networked UNIX mail systems and later the vast  “netnews” network.
The uucp network that lead to USENET began at Duke University and grew rapidly.  This user supported, phone based network carries mail and the netnews distributed bulletin board, the largest computer conferencing system in the world.
Until SVR4, uucp was the only networking capability provided by AT&T’s versions of UNIX.

Portable
UNIX runs on systems ranging from 16-bit embedded microcontrollers up through the largest mainframes and supercomputers.

The IEEE POSIX specification defines the of the basic features of UNIX.  The POSIX standard further enhances the portability of UNIX applications.

This portability is possible because UNIX is written in a high level language, C, instead of assembly.

Starting a UNIX Session
UNIX users are given a login name and a password.
The login name identifies you to the system
The password assures the system that you are who you claim to be.

Your initial password will be assigned by the system administrator but you can change it at any time.

Logging into UNIX
Prior to login, you will be presented with the login prompt, which typically contains the system name.

	nssdcs login:

At this point, enter your login name.

	nssdcs login: williams
	Password:

The system will prompt for a password.  The characters of the password will not echo as you type them.

Logging into UNIX, Cont'd.
After a successful login, you will be shown a greeting and possibly a “message of the day”.  

A message may inform you that "You have mail."  

Finally, you will get a shell prompt, which defaults to $ or %, depending on your shell.

	%

The Shell
The shell  is the UNIX command interpreter.  It serves the same basic function as COMMAND.COM under DOS or DCL under VAX/VMS.

All of the programs you run will be started by issuing commands to the shell.

There are several shells in common use:

sh		The Bourne shell
csh		The C shell
ksh		The Korn shell

Under System V Release 4 ksh is the default shell.

Shell Command Syntax
Simple commands are run just by typing their name.

	% 		who
	kirk     		console 	Oct  6  9:22
	spock    	ttya    		Oct  6  8:07
	scott    		ttyp3   		Oct  5 22:20 	(eng.ncc1701.ufp)
	mccoy    	ttyp4   		Oct  6  8:03 		(med.ncc1701.ufp)
	williams 	ttyp8   		Oct  6 10:16 	(eng.ncc1701.ufp)


Many commands take arguments, often one or more filenames.

	% cd myprograms
	% sort mydata1 mydata2

Options vs Arguments
In addition to arguments, most commands have one or more options. 
Arguments usually specify the objects on which the command is to operate
Options affect the nature of the operation and usually begin with a dash (-).

The command below includes both options and arguments.

	% sort -n -r datafile1 datafile2

Most commands allow options to be either grouped or separated.

	% sort -rn datafile

The Standard Output
Programs that produce output typically write it to the
standard output.  By default, the standard output is the terminal screen.

	% sort animals
	aardvark
	cat
	gazelle
	tiger

The standard output can be made to go to into a file by
redirecting it with >

	% sort animals > sorted_animals

The Standard Input
Similarly, most programs read from the standard input, unless otherwise instructed.  The default standard input is the terminal keyboard.

	% sort
	gazelle
	aardvark
	cat
	tiger
	^D
	aardvark
	cat
	gazelle
	tiger

The standard input can also be redirected, using <

	% sort < animals
	aardvark
	cat
	gazelle
	tiger
Control D marks the end of input.

Appending
When redirecting the standard output to a file, if the file already exists, the new contents will replace the old.  It is also possible to append the new contents to the old.  This is done with the symbol >>

	% cat > party_guests
	samir
	george
	anne
	^D
	% cat >> party_guests
	grace
	rick
	^D
	%

Standard Error
In addition to the standard input and standard output, there is also a standard error output
Used for error messages.
Redirection of standard output does not affect standard error.

	% sort aminals > sorted_animals
	sort: aminals: file not found.

The standard error may also be redirected or combined with the standard output.
Under the Korn or Bourne shells, use 2>.
To combine standard error with standard output, use 2>&1.
Under the C Shell, use >&, which redirects both stdout and stderr.

	% sort aminals 2>&1 > sorted_animals

Pipes and Filters
It is possible to connect the standard output of one command to the standard input of another.  This is called a pipe.

	% who | sort
	kirk     		console 	Oct  6  9:22
	mccoy    	ttyp4   		Oct  6  8:03 		(med.ncc1701.ufp)
	scott    		ttyp3   		Oct  5 22:20 	(eng.ncc1701.ufp)
	spock    	ttya    		Oct  6  8:07
	williams 	ttyp8   		Oct  6 10:16 	(eng.ncc1701.ufp)

The concepts of standard input, standard output, and the pipe were fundamental to creating the “tool building” philosophy that is central to UNIX.

The UNIX File System
UNIX files are organized into a tree-structured hierarchy.  

Each user is given a spot in the tree that is his or her default directory at login time.  This is the user's home directory.

Users may create any arrangment of subdirectories they like under their home directory.

UNIX File Names
UNIX file names are versatile and nearly unrestricted.

They may contain almost any character
File names are case sensitive!  FooBar and foobar are different files!
They may be of almost any length (up to 255 characters on most systems).
'.' is not a special character in UNIX.  File names such as this.is.a.very.peculiar.file.name are permitted and not uncommon.

The UNIX File System Hierarchy
UNIX file name components are separated by slash characters (/).

A typical UNIX system has a file tree that looks like the following.

/ (root)
	bin/  Some programs live here
	usr/  System files for users are here
		bin/    	Lots of programs live here	
		lib/    	C libraries, special programs
		local/  	Locally developed packages
		etc/    	System administration programs
	etc/   System configuration files
	home/  User's home directories (sometimes /user or /u)
		williams/
		kirk/
		spock/
		mccoy/
		scotty/

File Name Expansion(Wildcards)
The shell allows file names to be specified using a pattern.  The shell expands the pattern into the actual file names.  The process of expanding a file name pattern is called file name expansion (or, by old-timers, globbing).

The special characters used to construct file name patterns are ?, *, and [].

Wildcard Characters
The ? character matches any single character.

% ls foo.?
foo.h
foo.o
foo.c

The ? character can be used any where in the file name pattern and always matches exactly one character.

% ls ???.c
foo.c
bar.c
zap.c

Wildcard Characters,Cont'd.
The * character matches any group of zero or more characters.

% ls *.c
main.c
io.c
edit.c

Unlike DOS's filename wildcards, the * character can be used more than once in a pattern, and can be the first character.

% ls *cat*
catalog
concat.c
scatter_plots

Wildcard Characters,Cont'd.
The characters [] are used to surround character classes.  Each character class matches exactly one character.  Thus,

	% ls [fbm]oo

will match foo, boo, and moo, but not zoo.  A range of characters can be specified by separating the first and last character of the range with a hyphen.

	% ls [A-Z]*

This pattern matches all files that begin with an upper case letter.  Character classes may contain ‘-’, but not as the first character.

Common UNIX Commands
Below are some common UNIX commands.  Each command will be explained in detail later.

ls	List the contents of a directory
cd	Change to another directory
echo	Print text on screen
more	View a file
cat	Concatenate and print files
mv	Rename or move a file
cp	Copy a file
mkdir	Make a new directory
rmdir	Remove an empty directory

lsList Contents of a Directory
With no arguments, lists the names of all files in the current directory.  The list will be sorted down the columns by default.

   bin		mbox		projects
   calendar	mystuff	src

ls has a huge number of options.  A commonly used option is  -l, which produces a long listing.

   % ls -l
   -rw-r--r-- 1 		williams   	261 	Oct  3 08:28 	calendar
   -rw-rw-r-- 1 	williams 	17264 	Oct  6 13:17 	mbox

This listing gives the permission bits, the number of links, the file owner's name, the size of the file in bytes, the date and time it was last modified, and the file's name.

ls - More Options
File names that begin with a . are normally hidden and most programs ignore them.  (They are not matched by ‘*’ or ‘?’ in file name patterns.)  The -a option to ls will include these files in the output:

% ls -a
.   .cshrc		.profile	calendar
..  .login		bin		mbox

The -F option will print a character at the end of each file which identifies the file's type.  A directory is suffixed with /, an executable with *, a symbolic link with @, and a plain file is left alone.

% ls -F 
bin/		mbox	myprog*
calendar	mystuff/	myprog.c

cd and pwdChange to Another Directory
A cd by itself will take you to your home directory.
Under DOS, a plain cd prints your current directory.
Under UNIX, the pwd (print working directory) command will print the current directory.

% cd
% pwd
/home/staff/williams

Go to the directory src, in the current directory.
% cd src

Go to the directory immediately above this one.
% cd ..

mkdirMake a New Directory
mkdir is used to create a new directory.  The example below will make directories foo, bar, and baz, located in the current directory.  The current directory becomes their parent  directory.

% mkdir foo bar baz

New directories can be made anywhere you have the necessary permissions (i.e., you must have "write permission" on the parent directory).

% mkdir /tmp/jim

rmdirRemove a Directory
rmdir will remove an empty directory.  Only empty directories may be removed (but see rm -r, later).

% rmdir /tmp/jim tmp

To remove a directory, it must be empty and you must have write permission on the parent.  Some systems put further restrictions on file and directory removal.

echoPrint Text on Screen
The echo command causes its arguments to be printed on the screen.

% echo foo bar baz
foo bar baz

The -n option supresses the final newline, which is useful for prompts in shell scripts.

% echo -n "Enter name: "
Enter name: %

The System V R4 echo also supports several C-like escapes, which permit certain special effects.  Many UNIX purists hate this “feature”.

moreView a Text File
The more command is the most common program used for file viewing.

% more stuff.text

more will display one page at a time, waiting for the user to hit a key before going on to the next page.  DOS's crippled more is based on this program.

System V based systems have pg (for “page”), rather than more.  pg is very primitive compared to more.  A much better pager is the freely available less program. less is rather more than more, and quite a bit more than pg.  This can be confusing.

catConcatenate and Print Files
cat is used to combine, or concatenate, files, and send them to the standard output.
no pauses occur between screenfuls of text.
mostly used  to combine several files into one

% cat foo bar > foobar

Some versions of cat have options for printing tabs and newlines as visible characters and for other special effects.  Some UNIX purists hate these, usually the same ones who hate the System VR4 echo escapes.

catEntering Short Files
cat can also be used to enter a small amount of text into a file.  With no arguments, cat will read from the standard input.

% cat > shopping_list
milk
orange juice
apples
cereal
^D
%

mvMove or Rename Files
To rename a file, one moves it into a new name with mv.

% mv foo bar

Unlike DOS's ren command, the destination can be anywhere.

% mv shopping_list mystuff/shopping_list

If the destination is a directory that the user can write in,
then a file of the same name as the original is created.

% mv shopping_list mystuff
% ls mystuff
birthday_list	phonebook	shopping_list

mvMove or Rename Directories
mv can also rename or move directories.

% mv prog1 oldstuff/prog1

If the destination already exists and is a directory, then mv will make the source a sub-directory of the destination.

% mv prog1 oldstuff

mvOptions
If you mv a file on top of an already existing file, the old file is deleted, without warning.

% ls
bar foo
% mv foo bar
% ls
bar
	
The -i option will cause mv to ask permission before removing a file of the same name as the destination.

% mv -i foo bar
remove bar? y
%
Any response that begins with y counts as yes.

rmRemove Files
Use rm to remove one or more files.

% rm a b c

Filename expansion is both useful and dangerous with rm!

% rm *.o	
	
% rm * .o	
rm: .o: file not found

The -i option can be used to prevent such tragedies.  This
option will cause rm to prompt for confirmation before it removes each file.
YIKES!

rmRecursive Removal
rm also has the -r option, which causes rm to recursively remove all files and subdirectories, including hidden files.

	% rm -r oldstuff

Obviously, the combination of the -r option and filename wildcards is very dangerous and should be used with great caution.

cpCopying Files
cp  is used to make a copy of a file.

% cp foo bar 		

Multiple files can be copied into a subdirectory.

% cp foo.c bar.c baz.c backups

The above command copies the three .c files into the directory backups.  The new files will have the same names as the originals.  If backups doesn't exist, cp will complain.

cpOptions
cp can also act recursively, to copy an entire tree.

	% cp -R dir1 dir2

Like mv and rm, cp supports the  -i option.

The -p option to cp will set the modification time of the copy to be the same as that of the original.  By default, the modification time of the copy will be the current time.  -p also tries to set the permission bits on the copy to be the same as on the original.

File Ownership
All files under UNIX have an owner and a group.  The owner and group for a file are found in a long ls listing.

% ls -lg
total 47
drwxrwsr-x 	3 williams staff    	512 	Oct  6 13:41 	./
drwxrwsr-x  	4 williams staff    	512 	Jul 17 09:46 	../
drwxrwsr-x 	2 williams staff    	512 	Oct  6 11:02 	bin
-rw-rw-r--  	1 williams staff   	1194 	Sep  9 13:27 	calendar
-rw-rw-r--  	1 williams staff  	17264 	Oct  6 13:17 	mbox
drwxrwxr-x  	1 williams staff    	161 	Oct  5 16:18 	mystuff

The files above are owned by williams in the group staff. 
A file is owned by the user who creates it.
The initial group of a file depends on several things.
File ownership can be changed with the chown command.
File group can be changed with with chgrp command.

File Access
% ls -l
total 47
drwxrwsr-x  	3 williams staff    512 	Oct  6 13:41 	./
drwxrwsr-x  	4 williams staff    512 	Jul 17 09:46 	../
drwxr-sr-x  	2 williams staff    512 	Oct  6 11:02 	bin
-rw-rw-r--  	1 williams staff   1194 	Sep  9 13:27 	calendar
-rw-------  	1 williams staff  17264 	Oct  6 13:17 	mbox
drwxrwxr-x  	1 williams staff    161 	Oct  5 16:18 	mystuff

In a long listing the first group of characters gives each file's permission bits, which define the access rights to the file.

The first character gives the file's type, the next nine give the file’s access permissions for the owner, the group, and others.
- is used for a plain file, d is used for a directory, l is used for a symbolic link.
r, indicates read permission, w indicates write permission, x and s indicate execute permission.

chmod
The chmod command is used to change the permission bits (the mode) of a file.  There are two different styles of argument to chmod.  The first style, used by old-timers and programmers, uses octal numbers to change the mode of a file.

% chmod 644 myfile

This sets myfile to have permissions -rw-r--r--.  The other option syntax uses symbolic values and is a bit more user friendly.

% chmod a=r myfile		everyone gets just read permission
% chmod ug+w myfile	owner (user) and group get write permission
% chmod go-x myprog	group and others have no execute permission

GroupsThe Old Way
At any given time, a user is “in” exactly one group.

New files and directories are given the group ID of the user when the user creates the file. 
The newgroup command allows the user to switch amongst any of the groups for which the user is authorized.
Doesn’t work well for users who work on many projects.

GroupsThe New Way
Starting with about BSD 4.1, a new method of setting the group ID was introduced which facilitated working on many projects at once.

New files and directories are given the group ID of the directory in which they are created.
Users are always “in” all the groups they are authorized for so newgroup command is not needed.
Group ID is a property of location, not the creator.

GroupsEvery Which Way
When the BSD and System V variants of UNIX were merged, some compromise on groups had to be made.  The solution allows both sorts of behavior, but is a little complex.

Any directory with the set group id bit not set uses Old Way semantics.  Files created there will get the group id  of the creator.
Any directory with the set group id bit set uses New Way semantics.  Files created there will have the group id of the parent directory.
In both cases, a new directory has its set group id bit set the same as the parent directory.

Shell Variables
The shell maintains certain information in its own variables.  Shell variables affect how the shell searches for commands, set the shell's prompt, and otherwise customize its behavior.  Under sh and ksh, shell variables are set by following them with an equal sign (=) and the value to be set.

Note that NO SPACE is allowed on either side of the =.  To see what variables are set, use the

Environment variables
Shell variables affect only the shell and how it interprets your commands.  Programs you run can not access shell variables.  There is a separate set of variables, called the environment, that any program can access.  All shells provide commands for manipulating these environment variables.

To see all currently set environment variables, use printenv.

Both shell and environment variables are referenced by preceding the name with a $.

Quoting
The shell interprets some characters specially.  To include these characters as arguments or options to a command, they must be quoted.  There are several quoting mechanisms, each of which serves a distinct purpose.  The simplest quoting method is to enclose the argument in single quote marks (').

	% echo 'this is a single argument'
	% grep '*foo*' list

Filename expansion characters such as *, ?, [ and ] lose their special meaning inside single quotes.

Quoting, Cont'd.
Inside of single quote marks ('), shell and environment variables are not expanded.

% echo 'your home directory is $HOME'
your home directory is $HOME

If double quotes (") are used, then shell and environment variables are expanded.

% echo "your home directory is $HOME"
your home directory is /home/williams

Tilde expansion
In the Korn or C shells, the tilde character (~) can be used as a convenient short hand for home directories.  When a tilde is at the beginning of a word, and the next character is a /, the tilde is replaced by the contents of $home, your home directory.  The following command sets the current directory to $home/mystuff.

% cd ~/mystuff

If the tilde is followed by a user name, it is replaced by that user's home directory.  The command below copies the file engine_specs from user scotty's home directory and puts the copy in my directory mystuff.

% cp ~scotty/engine_specs mystuff

When a Bourne or Korn shells start up, it looks to see if a file named .profile exists in the user's home directory. The C shell also allows customization, but since it has a different syntax for many functions, it uses the files .cshrc and .login for customization.

Regular Expressions
Several UNIX commands make use of the concept of a regular expression. Regular expressions are similar to filename wildcards, but much more powerful.  All of the standard editors use regular expressions, as well as commands such as grep, awk, and sed.  A solid understanding of regular expressions is vital to making full use of UNIX.

Single Character REs
A single character matches itself.

	a

The character . matches any single character.

	.

Character Class REs
A set of characters in a brackets ([]) matches any one of those characters.

	[abcd] - matches a, b, c, or d

Ranges are specified by using - to separate the first and last character in the range.

	[a-z] - matches any lowercase letter

If the first character is ^, then the range is complemented.

	[^1234567890] - matches any character that is not 					a digit

More Complex REs
For any regular expressions re, re1, and re2, the following are valid combinations.

re1re2		- matches a match for re1, followed by a match for re2
re*		- matches 0 or more occurances of re
re{m-n}	- a range of repetitions, at least m, but no more then n
^re		- re must be at the beginning of the line
re$		- re must be at the end of the line
\(re\)		- label
\n		- back reference to label n, in the range 1-9

A regular expression always matches the longest string possible.

RE Examples
[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z_0-9]*

Matches any letter or underscore, followed by any number of
letters, digits or underscores.

[0-9][0-9]*[A-Za-z]*[0-9][0-9]*

Matches at least one digit, followed by any number of letters
(including none), followed by another sequence of digits.

\([0-9][0-9]*\)[A-Za-z]*\1

Matches at least one digit, followed by any number of letters,
followed by exactly the same sequence of digits.

grep
The grep command is used to search one or more files for lines matching a regular expression.  For a simple string, the command would be a follows.

% grep Galileo data.1 data.2 data.3

Regular expressions that contain special characters must be quoted, so that the shell doesn't give the characters its own special meanings.

% grep '[aeiou].*[^aeiou]' wordlist

The name grep comes from the equivalent editor command, g/RE/p, which means to globally search for the given RE and print each matching line.

egrep
The egrep command supports extensions to the regular expression syntax.

re+	- one or more repetitions
re?	- zero or one repetitions
       - alternation

The egrep command does  not allow back references via \n.  Parentheses may be used for grouping.

% egrep 'Galileo|Viking' data.1 data.2

An egrep Example
To practice an extended pattern that contains a few of the 
pattern-matching characters +, ?, I, (, and ), enter:

egrep “\( *([a-xA-X]*I [0-9]*)” mygrepfile.txt

This displays lines that contain letters in parentheses or digits
in parentheses, but not parenthisized letter - digit combinations.  It matches t and 873902, but not beta18b.

Note that the reverse slash matches parentheses but without it both parentheses are used as a part of an expression (opposite to grep).

Foreground vsBackground
Normally, UNIX programs are run in the foreground, which means that the user must wait for one command to finish before entering another.  If you wish to run a command that will take a long time,  you can put the command in the background, which allows you to get on with other work.

% sort -o output very_long_file
% edit report

To put a command in background, end it with an &. The process ID of the command will be printed.

10324
% edit report

To see what processes you have running use the ps command.

6542 p0 R      0:00 sort very_long_file
6543 p0 R      0:00 ps

kill
Sometimes it is necessary to terminate a process that is hung, or running amok, or otherwise has become undesirable.  The kill command is provided for this.  

% kill 1283

The above command will send the KILL signal to process 1283.  Other signals are possible.  They
are given as options to kill.

% kill -TERM 1283

The  TERM signal allows the application to clean up before quitting.  The default KILL signal halts an application without notice.

Job Control
Under traditional UNIX, once a command has been started in foreground or background, that's where it stays until completion.  Berkeley UNIX introduced the notion of job control, which allows processes to be moved from foreground to background while they are running.  Job control is available in the Berkeley C shell and the Korn shell.

A job that is currently running in foreground can be stopped  by typing ^Z.  Once a job is stopped, it can be restarted in either the foreground or background with the fg or bg commands, respectively.  The jobs command displays the status of all current processes.

Job Control Example
% sort bigfile.1 > sorted.1 &
[1] 18828
% sort bigfile.2 > sorted.2
^Z
% jobs
[2]   + Stopped sort bigfile.2 > sorted.2
[1]   - Running sort bigfile.1 > sorted.1
% bg
[2]   sort -o bigfile.2 > sorted.2
% jobs
[1]     Running sort bigfile.2 > sorted.2
[2]   + Running sort bigfile.1 > sorted.1
% fg %1
sort bigfile.1 > sorted.1
% kill %2
[2]   Terminated   sort bigfile.2 > sorted.2

Shell Scripts
The UNIX shells all allow for the creation and execution of shell scripts, which are simply files that contain lists of commands for the shell to run.  Unlike .BAT files  under DOS, or .COM files under VMS, there is no special extension required on UNIX shell script files.  It is, however, necessary to set the execute permission bit on a shell script file, or the shell will not execute the script.

Sample Shell Script
All shell scripts should start with the characters #!, followed by the name of the shell for which the script was written.  Since the different shells have different syntaxes, this prevents errors caused when the wrong shell tries to execute a given script.


#!/bin/sh
#
# This is a korn shell script.
# A pound sign (#) begins a comment, which
# extends to the end of the line.
echo -n "Today is "
date
echo "The users currently logged in are:"
users

Control Flow in Scripts
Shell scripts often make use of control flow statements such as those found in high level languages.

#!/bin/sh
# This script removes .o files that are
# older than the corresponding .c file.

for cf in *.c
do
	of=${cf%.c}.o
	if [ -e $of -a $of -ot $cf ]
	then
		echo "Removing " $of
		rm $of
	fi
done

Parameters
Shell scripts can take arguments and options just like programs.  These are called the positional parameters and  are refered to in the script by the variable names $1 through $9.  The number of positional parameters passed to a script is given by $#.  Parameter $0 is the name of the script.  The first argument is in $1. Under the Bourne shell, parameters beyond $9 must be accessed via the shift command, which shifts arguments left by one, starting with $1.  Under the Korn shell, arguments beyond $9 require braces, for example, ${16}.

Shells have variables (parameters) like other languages
Positional Parameters:    $1, $2, ..., $9

Variables are assigned with an equals sign
No spaces are allowed before or after the equals sign

Exporting Shell Variables
Variables are associated with the shell that creates them, not subshells (like shell scripts)

$ echo $x
Hello
$ sh		# Run a new shell
$ echo $x	# Variable x isn’t there!

$ exit		# Leave the subshell

$ export x
$ sh
$ echo $x
Hello
$ exit

Modifying Shell VariablesThe . command
The . (dot) command will run a shell script in the current shell, not in a subshell
Commonly used to reexecute the .profile startup script without logging in again

$ echo $x		# What is x now?

$ echo $x		# See?  It didn't change in the current shell
Hello
$ . chvar Goodbye		# Now execute chvar in the current shell
Goodbye
$ echo $x		# And x actually gets changed

Filters
Filters are programs that accept data on standard input, process it, and write the modified data to standard output.
How many unique lines are in all of my data files?

grep is one of the most often used filters

Has many options for altering the kind of output generated
sed and awk are general purpose programmable filters

awk, named after the authors, is a more complete programming language, including variables, arithmetic, control flow, etc.

Combining many small filters is easier than programming one big one

awk pattern scanning and processing language
awk overcomes some of the limitations of sed
arithmetic and builtin functions
variables and arrays
control flow (if, for, while)
Basic awk  programs are lists of patterns and actions, which are applied to each line of the input in turn
pattern { action }
pattern { action }
Patterns in awk can be regular expressions, ala sed
$ awk '/[^ ]@[^ ]/ { print }' mail.msg

$ awk 'NF == 1 { print $1 }' test.dat

awk(continued)
awk automatically splits each input line into fields, called $1, $2, ... $NF, where NF is a variable set to the total number of fields.
Here is an easier way to print the login times and userids from our exercise in sed programming:
$ who | awk '{ print $5, $1 }'
The -Fc switch sets the field delimiter from whitespace (blanks and tabs) to the character c
$ awk -F: '{ print $1, $7 }' /etc/passwd
prints userids and the shells they use
Two special "patterns", BEGIN and END match the beginning and end of the file, respectively
Normally used for initialization and cleanup

awk Arrays
Arrays are allowed as in other languages
$ cat backwards
# backwards: print output in reverse line order
awk '{ line[NR] = $0 }
END  { for (i = NR; i > 0; i--) print line[i] }' $*
Associative arrays are indexed by strings rather than by numbers
$ cat wordfreq
# wordfreq: print word counts from input
awk '{ for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) num[$i]++ }
END  { for (word in num) print num[word], "  ", word } 
' $* | sort -nr

Traps: catching interrupts
If a shell script is interrupted by a ^C or some other signal, any temporary files will be left behind
Need to "catch" the interrupt signal, cleanup anything that needs it, and exit
Basic command:
trap sequence-of-commands list-of-signal-numbers
Example: clean up a temporary file on receiving an interrupt or terminate signal
trap 'rm -f /tmp/tmpfile; exit 1' 1 15

Shell Signal Numbers
0		shell exit (for any reason, including end of file)
1		hangup
2		interrupt (^C)
3		quit (^\; causes program to produce core dump)
9		kill (cannot be caught or ignored)
15	terminate, default signal generated by kill(1)

Aliases
Most implementations of shells allow for aliases
Commonly used to set default switches for commands
alias ls='ls -F'
alias ll='ls -l'
alias rm='rm -i'
Can be used to string several commands together
alias dir='pwd; ls -l'
alias logout='clear; exit'
alias whoops='ps -axu | grep'
Any arguments following the alias are appending to the replacement text after the alias is expanded
However, there is no mechanism for using arguments within the replacement text
If arguments are needed, use a shell function

Shell Functions
Modern versions of the Bourne shell allow functions
Functions store a series of commands for later execution
Functions declared in .profile are available as interactive commands, like aliases
Functions are executed in the context of the current shell; not a subshell
Arguments to the function become positional parameters, $1, $2, ...
After the function exits, the original positional parameters are restored
Variables local to the function can be declared by “local” builtin command
These variables exist only during the execution of the function

Example Shell Function(continued)
Repeat a command:  
Usage:  repeat n  command
e.g.:       repeat 80 echo -n "-"
	  repeat()
{
	local count=$1
	shift
	while [ "$count" -gt 0 ]
	do
 		$*
 		count=`expr $count - 1`
	done
}
Note:  This function is really slow.  Repeated arithmetic with expr takes a lot of CPU time.
